knowledge_type_note: Names a board feature. That rooks belong on open files is a related rule of thumb, not part of the definition.

attributions.note: My System devotes early chapters to the open file — its genesis, its purpose, obstacles to a file operation, and the outpost as its natural consequence.

history.notes: Rooks on open files were understood long before Nimzowitsch; what he supplied was systematic treatment and the link to the outpost. Not a claim of invention.

development.change: Systematic treatment; the file is tied to the outpost and to provoking pawn weaknesses.
Quantified: open-file bonuses of roughly 8-20 centipawns, with extra for doubling and for bearing on the enemy king.

engine_era_note: Uncontroversial and directly quantified in engine evaluation. The engine-era refinement is that the bonus is conditional — larger when the file bears on the enemy king, and worth little without an entry square.

preconditions: A file contains no pawns of either colour (open), or pawns of one colour only (half-open for the other side)
indicators_for: A safe entry square exists on the seventh or eighth rank, or on any rank the defender cannot cover
The file leads towards the enemy king
Rooks can be doubled on it, or a queen placed behind them
The opponent cannot contest the file, or contesting it costs them something
indicators_against: Every entry square on the file is defended — the rook stares and does nothing
The opponent can contest the file and trade all the rooks off
The file can be closed by a pawn advance
Occupying it costs a tempo the position cannot spare
false_positive_traps: REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: a file with no pawns is not automatically useful. Without an entry square, a rook on it accomplishes nothing.
Detecting 'no pawns on this file' is trivial and fires constantly. The reportable fact is the file PLUS a usable entry square.
Contested files where all rooks come off leave neither side with anything.
An open file is not an advantage on its own. In a proven test position with a rook of each colour on the open d-file, the evaluation is +0.02 - the file belongs to nobody.

typical_plans: Double rooks on the file, then invade on the seventh
Half-open file: pile onto the enemy pawn standing on it
Create the entry square first by exchanging its defender
Open a file deliberately with a pawn break aimed at the enemy king
typical_moves: Rook to the file, then doubling; a rook lift to the third rank and across
typical_pawn_structures: Half-open d-file in front of a backward d-pawn
typical_piece_arrangements: Doubled rooks, or queen behind rook, on one file
tactical_consequences: Invasion on the seventh rank; back-rank threats
strategic_consequences: Files are how heavy pieces enter a position at all

exceptions: A file with no entry squares is worth nothing.
A half-open file can be more valuable than a fully open one, because the enemy pawn on it is a fixed target and the file cannot be neutralised by a simple rook trade.
Nimzowitsch's usage of the term differs from the modern one.
limitations: The feature is trivially detectable and therefore trivially over-reportable. Usability is the whole question.
misconceptions: That rooks belong on open files unconditionally. They belong on files they can invade down.
That an open file is better than a half-open one.

examples.note:
A QUIET position from a master game — after Rxe5, ply 60 — in which the c- and e-files are open, and White's rook on c1 and White's rook on e1 and Black's rook on e8 and Black's rook on e5 stand on it. Quiet here has a mechanical meaning: the side to move has no check and no capture that wins material, so the next move has to be chosen on positional grounds. That matters because this base's other corpus is 788 tactical puzzles, in which a positional feature cannot be isolated.

WHAT IS VERIFIED: the game replays legally end to end through the page's own move generator, so the FEN is derived rather than transcribed; and the feature is present by mechanical measurement in lib/features.js.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: that the concept decides this position, or that the players were thinking about it. Note also a limitation of method — the position was FOUND by this system's own Layer 4, so it demonstrates the concept and cannot by itself validate the matcher that found it. Other concepts licensed here: passed-pawn, isolated-queen-pawn, doubled-pawns, bishop-pair.

counterexamples.note: A symmetric position with the d-file open and a rook of each colour already on it. Constructed to isolate the file itself: if an open file were an advantage, occupying one could not leave the position dead level.

engine.verdict_note: Dead level at +0.02, with the best line trading the rooks off immediately. An open file is not an advantage in itself - it is an advantage only when one side can use it and the other cannot, and here both can equally. This is the position behind the open-file-not-useful false-positive case, and it is why this system reports a file as open rather than as good.

by_level.beginner: There are no pawns on that file, so a rook there can see all the way down the board.
by_level.intermediate: The {file}-file is open. Before committing the rook, find the square you intend to invade on — a file with no entry point does nothing.
by_level.advanced: Open file with an entry square on {square}. Double, or place the queen behind, and check whether the opponent can contest and trade off.
by_level.master: File plus entry point, always. A half-open file with a fixed enemy pawn on it is frequently worth more than a fully open one, because it cannot be neutralised by an exchange of rooks.

by_depth.normal: The {file}-file is open. That matters because there is an entry square on {square} — a file a rook cannot invade down is not worth occupying.
by_depth.deep: A file with no pawns of either colour; half-open means pawns of one colour only, and is the natural file to attack down since the enemy pawn is a fixed target. Nimzowitsch treated the open file systematically and tied it to the outpost — the file supports a piece planted in enemy territory, and driving that piece off with a pawn is what damages the file in turn. The qualification that matters in practice is the entry square: engine evaluation gives a rook on an open file only about 8 to 20 centipawns, which is the right order of magnitude for the feature by itself. What makes a file decisive is somewhere to go.

explanations.lesson: An open file is a road. Before you drive down it, check there is somewhere to arrive.

beginner_words: the rook can see down the board

definition_short: A file with no pawns of either colour, which rooks and queens can use to exert pressure and invade.
definition_long:
A file with no pawns on it at all. A HALF-OPEN (or SEMI-OPEN) file has pawns of one colour only — half-open for the side without a pawn there, and the natural file to attack down, because the enemy pawn on it is a target.

The critical qualification, and the one most often left out: a file is worth having only if it offers an ENTRY SQUARE. A rook on an open file whose seventh and eighth ranks are all covered controls squares and achieves nothing. The plan is always file plus entry point, not file alone.

Nimzowitsch treated the open file as a subject in its own right and tied it to the outpost: the file is what supports a piece planted in enemy territory, and driving that piece away with a pawn is what damages the file. Note a terminology difference — he used '(semi) open file' even for rooks standing in front of their own pawn chain, which modern usage would not.

Engine evaluation gives a rook on an open file a bonus of roughly 8 to 20 centipawns, which is a useful calibration: real, worth having, and far smaller than a pawn.
